area: Area VII. Slow Flight and Stalls
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the aerodynamics of flight just above the stall warning, including the region of reversed command and the shifting stall speed, and fly coordinated slow flight in whatever configuration the examiner names within commercial tolerances (altitude plus or minus 50 feet, heading plus or minus 10°, airspeed +5/-0 knots, bank plus or minus 5°) with no stall warning.
why: Every takeoff, approach and go-around passes through low speed and high angle of attack, and slow flight is where you learn that regime at a safe height [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. A commercial pilot meets it heavy, hot, busy and close to the ground, so you need to sense how near the critical AOA you are before a buffet or a horn tells you [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

prereading.what: Coordinated flight, AOA, slow flight, how to fly it and its ten common errors. Read this first.

prereading.label: AFH 5-13 to 5-16

prereading.what: The throttle and elevator as energy controls, and the front side and backside of the power curve.
prereading.label: AFH 4-4 to 4-5

prereading.what: Energy errors and how an airplane slides into an irreversible deceleration or sink rate.
prereading.label: AFH 4-12 to 4-17

prereading.what: Stalls, why the stall speed is not fixed, and AOA indicators with their limits.
prereading.label: PHAK 5-25 to 5-28

prereading.what: The four parts of the left-turning tendency: torque reaction, slipstream, gyroscopic action and P-factor.

warmup: Think first: in the landing configuration the sample airplane in the PHAK stalls at 47 knots with power on but at 57 knots with power off. You are flying slow flight at 54 knots with plenty of power. What happens if you pull the throttle to idle and hold your altitude with back pressure? And why does slowing down from here take more power, not less?

key_terms.def: Flight at an airspeed where any further increase in AOA or load factor, or any reduction in power, would bring on a stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

The AOA where airflow separates and the wing stalls, about 16° to 20° depending on design. For a given configuration the airplane always stalls at this same AOA [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]] [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]].
The published stall speed. It holds only in unaccelerated, coordinated flight at one weight and one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
The speed at which a natural or artificial stall warning begins [[60:21|14 CFR 1.2]].
Speeds where holding altitude at a lower airspeed takes a higher power setting [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].
In the region of reverse command, a disturbance that lowers airspeed raises total drag, which lowers airspeed further [[24:386|AFH G-14]].
Power available minus power required. Above zero the airplane can climb or turn while holding speed; below zero it must lose energy [[24:91|AFH 4-5]] [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].
Altitude and airspeed off in the same direction (lower and slower, or higher and faster). Corrected mainly with the throttle [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Altitude and airspeed off in opposite directions (higher and slower, or lower and faster). Corrected mainly with the elevator [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].
Knowing the margin between the current AOA and the critical AOA, which an AOA indicator displays [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
At high AOA the downgoing blade on the right of the propeller disc makes more thrust than the upgoing blade, yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
The spiraling slipstream that pushes sideways on the vertical fin, strongest at high power and low forward speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

chunks.title: Slow flight at the commercial standard

body.p: Slow flight is flight at an airspeed where any further increase in AOA, any increase in load factor, or any reduction in power would bring on a stall warning such as buffet or a horn. When a warning does come, you correct for it at once [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. You practice it at altitude so that the feel, sound and sight of low-speed, high-AOA flight are familiar before you meet them near the ground [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

For training and testing the AFH gives slow flight two parts. First, slowing to, maneuvering at and recovering from a speed that keeps the stall warning silent, with 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed as a good target. Second, flying it in the configurations used for takeoff, climb, descent, approach and go-around [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. It is usually evaluated in the landing configuration, but clean and takeoff configurations may be evaluated too [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

Only the heading window stays the same. Altitude, airspeed and bank windows are cut in half. The examiner specifies the configuration, altitude, heading and bank (ACS CA.VII.A.S4, S5). The slow side of the airspeed window is zero at both levels, so one knot below the target is already a deviation.

callout.text: No stall warning: S4 asks for coordinated straight-and-level flight, turns, climbs and descents without a stall warning (ACS CA.VII.A.S4). The ACS Appendix 3 note adds that turbulence may cause a momentary stall horn. If you recognize it and correct promptly, that alone is not unsatisfactory; continual deviation, no correction or no recognition is (ACS CA.VII.A, Appendix 3).
Commercial habit: brief your numbers out loud before you slow down, for example 'Target 55, altitude 3,500, heading 270, full flaps.' You and the examiner then share the same window.

check.q: The examiner asks for slow flight at 55 knots. Which airspeeds meet the commercial standard?
check.a: 55 to 60 knots, the specified speed +5/-0 (ACS CA.VII.A.S5), with no stall warning (ACS CA.VII.A.S4).

chunks.title: Angle of attack, airspeed and lift

body.p: Lift depends on AOA and airspeed together. A large AOA at low airspeed makes the same lift as a small AOA at high airspeed [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]]. The figure shows one wing holding level flight at three speeds: about 3° at high speed, 6° at cruise and 12° at low speed [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]].

The lift equation shows why the AOA has to grow so much. Lift is proportional to the square of velocity: at the same AOA, 200 knots gives four times the lift of 100 knots [[1:101|PHAK 5-4]]. Turned around (application): to hold the same lift at half the speed, the wing needs four times the lift coefficient, which it gets from a higher AOA. The limit is the critical AOA [[1:101|PHAK 5-4]].

Each airplane stalls at one critical AOA, roughly 16° to 20° depending on design [[1:122|PHAK 5-25]]. For a given configuration it does not change with weight, bank angle, temperature, density altitude or CG [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]]. The stall speed moves with all of those; the stalling AOA does not. That is why a stall comes from exceeding the critical AOA, not from low airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

bullets: At high AOA, small AOA changes cause big drag changes [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]]. In slow flight a small pitch change makes a large airspeed change [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
In the PHAK sample wing, L/D peaks near 6° AOA and lift peaks at 20°, its critical AOA [[1:102|PHAK 5-5]].

Nose-high and slow, part of the thrust points upward and helps hold the airplane up, so wing loading is less than you would expect [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]]. Application: take that power away and the wing has to carry more of the weight.
The PHAK asks for extra vigilance at low thrust and low speed, and says to use an AOA indicator if one is installed [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]].

callout.text: Same wing, same critical AOA, every time. What moves is the airspeed at which you reach it.

check.q: Your airplane is 400 lb lighter than on your last flight. Does its critical AOA change?
check.a: No. The critical AOA does not change with weight; only the speed at which you reach it changes [[1:124|PHAK 5-27]].

chunks.title: Why stall speed moves: load, power, flaps, weight and CG

body.p: The published 1G stall speed is true only in unaccelerated flight, coordinated, at one weight (usually maximum gross) and one CG (usually most forward) [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Slow flight changes several of those at once.
This sample stall speed table for a 2,750 lb airplane shows three effects at once [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]:

bullets: Gear and flaps down lower the stall speed. Power off and wings level: 65 knots clean, 57 knots in the landing configuration [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].
Power on lowers it again. Landing configuration, wings level: 57 knots power off, 47 knots power on [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].
Bank raises it. Landing configuration, power off: 57 knots level, 62 at 30°, 68 at 45° and 81 at 60° [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

body.p: Bank works through load factor, which is a trigonometric relationship [[1:130|PHAK 5-33]]. Stall speed rises with the square root of the load factor [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]], and a level 60° bank gives 2 G and a stall speed 41 percent above the 1G value [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. The table agrees: 65 knots x 1.414 = 91.9, and it shows 92 knots at 60° clean, power off [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].

head: Factor
Effect on the stall
rows: Higher stall speed; the wing needs more AOA for the extra lift [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]
Higher stall speed from the higher wing loading, and more back-elevator force [[1:141|PHAK 5-44]]
Less elevator needed to reach the stall, so an accidental stall comes easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]]
Little or no change in indicated stall speed; true airspeed is higher [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]
Higher stall speed, even from a small amount [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]

callout.text: Application: this table explains why S3 lists a reduction in power as one of the three triggers. With flaps down you can be flying above the 47-knot power-on stall speed of this sample airplane but below its 57-knot power-off stall speed. Pull the power and hold altitude and the margin is gone. Read your own POH table the same way.

check.q: Using the table, landing configuration and power on, what is the stall speed in a 30° bank?

body.p: In normal command, holding altitude, a higher airspeed takes a higher power setting and a lower airspeed a lower one. In the region of reversed command it flips: a higher airspeed takes less power and a lower airspeed takes more power to hold altitude. That does not mean cutting power makes you slower in some simple way [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].

On the PHAK power required curve, the region runs from the lowest point of the curve, the best endurance speed, down to the stall or minimum control speed [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]] [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]]. Near the stall, the power needed for level flight is quite high [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. Slow flight lives inside this region.

bullets: Pitch becomes the more effective control of airspeed, and power the control of the flightpath [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Speed instability: if turbulence knocks the speed down, it may keep falling unless you reduce the AOA or add power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
Short-field power approach: a high sink rate may be stopped with power. Lowering the nose without power gives a rapid sink and altitude loss [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

Soft-field climb: climbing out of ground effect before reaching normal climb attitude and speed can leave the airplane unable to climb even at full power; the only way out is lowering the nose, which costs altitude [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

body.p: The AFH shows the same trap at a high, hot airport. With less power available, the airplane slows from point 1, where it climbs (A), to point 2, where it stops climbing (B), to point 3, where the stall horn sounds and power available is less than power required (C) [[24:102|AFH 4-16]]. The caption notes the airport sits at 7,820 ft on a hot afternoon [[24:101|AFH 4-15]].

callout.text: The AFH fix is not intuitive: give up some altitude to gain speed, until power available is again more than power required, then climb (at VX if terrain is rising) or turn back to the airport [[24:102|AFH 4-16]] [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

check.q: You are below the best endurance speed and want to fly 5 knots slower while staying level. Do you add or reduce power?
check.a: Add power. In the region of reversed command a lower airspeed needs a higher power setting to hold altitude [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].

chunks.title: Energy management at the slow edge

body.p: The AFH treats the throttle as the total energy control and the elevator as the control that splits energy between altitude and airspeed. Neither one controls altitude or airspeed by itself [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

The catch near the stall: more throttle helps only if there is excess power. Slow enough, even full throttle may give none. Then the first move is forward pressure to cut AOA and induced drag, and only then power [[24:99|AFH 4-13]]. On the backside of the curve, a little forward pressure moves the airplane toward the middle of the curve, where excess power returns [[24:91|AFH 4-5]].

Application to the checkride: with only 50 feet and +5/-0 knots to work with (ACS CA.VII.A.S5), catch errors while they are small. Twenty feet high and 2 knots slow is a distribution error, so a small forward pressure fixes both. Twenty feet low and 2 knots slow is a total energy error, so you need power.

callout.text: AFH examples of slipping into irreversible deceleration or sink rate: slow, unstable approaches; go-arounds with the gear or flaps left down; and steeper-than-normal turns in the pattern [[24:103|AFH 4-17]].

check.q: In slow flight you are 30 feet high and 3 knots slow. What kind of energy error is it, and which control fixes it?
check.a: A distribution error (higher and slower). Use the elevator: a little forward pressure trades the extra altitude for speed [[24:98|AFH 4-12]].

chunks.title: Yaw effects: why the right rudder grows

body.p: Near the 1G stall at high power, torque, slipstream and P-factor can make a strong left yaw, and the closer you are to the stall, the more right rudder you need [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. The PHAK calls the whole left-turning tendency 'torque' and breaks it into four elements [[1:127|PHAK 5-30]]:

bullets: Torque reaction: the engine turns the propeller one way and the airplane tries to roll the other way. Rigging usually compensates at cruise speed, where most flying happens, not at slow-flight power and speed [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

Corkscrew slipstream: at high power and low forward speed the spiral is compact and pushes hard on the vertical fin. The PHAK notes its rolling moment is to the right while torque reaction acts to the left, so one may partly counter the other [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
Gyroscopic action: a force on the propeller disc acts 90° ahead in the direction of rotation, so pitch changes cause yaw and yaw causes pitch [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
P-factor: at high AOA the downgoing right blade meets the air at a higher resultant velocity and makes more thrust, so the nose yaws left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

body.p: Adverse yaw adds to the workload. When you roll, the rising wing gets more lift and more drag, so the nose yaws away from the turn; rudder applied with the aileron cancels it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. At low speed the controls are less effective and need larger movements [[24:114|AFH 5-9]], so expect larger rudder inputs too.

Power changes are where you feel it. Adding power for a climb increases the yawing tendency, which you counter with rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Application: reducing power for a descent eases that yaw, so you need less right rudder.

callout.text: Power up, right foot in. Power down, right foot out. The ball stays centered.

check.q: Why does P-factor grow in slow flight?
check.a: It comes from flying at a high AOA. The unbalanced thrust shrinks as the propeller shaft lines up with the airflow and grows as the AOA rises [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

chunks.title: Uncoordinated flight next to the critical AOA

body.p: Coordinated flight means the nose is yawed straight into the relative wind and the ball is centered [[24:113|AFH 5-8]]. The main cause of an inadvertent spin is exceeding the critical AOA while using too much or too little rudder, and to a lesser extent aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]]. Slow flight keeps you a few degrees from that AOA for minutes at a time.

bullets: Skidding turn (aileron and rudder the same way): a resulting spin rotates in the direction the controls are applied [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].
Slipping turn (opposite aileron held against the rudder): a resulting spin usually goes opposite to the aileron [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].
Uncoordinated flight makes the airspeed indicator and altimeter unreliable, so the stall warning may be your first clue [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].
Classic setups: go-arounds and short-field takeoffs at high pitch, high power and low speed, and skidding base-to-final turns [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

body.p: Aileron near the stall has its own trap. A down aileron raises that wing's AOA. If a wing drops at the stall and you use aileron to pick it up, you can deepen the stall on that wing and roll further. Reduce the AOA first, then roll [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

callout.text: In slow flight, rudder is not optional. With the ball out, the airspeed you are watching may already be wrong [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

check.q: During a slow-flight left turn you hold too much left rudder. Which way would a spin most likely go?
check.a: To the left. In a skid, rotation is in the direction the controls are applied [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

chunks.title: Stall warning and AOA indicators: range and limits

body.p: A normal category airplane must have a clear and distinctive stall warning with enough margin to prevent an inadvertent stall [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]. VSW is the speed where natural or artificial stall warning begins [[60:21|14 CFR 1.2]]. Certification lets the warning come from natural pre-stall buffet or from a device, and most vintage airplanes and many light-sport and experimental airplanes have no device [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

head: Cue
Range and limits
rows: Many devices warn 4 to 8 knots before the stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]]. Where it is required equipment, do not deactivate it for a practical test [[13:22|AC 61-67C p16]].
Less noticeable power-off than power-on. In a power-off 1G stall the main cue may be full up elevator and a high descent rate [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].
Less resistance, larger movements and slower response as speed drops [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
Less air noise; a fixed-pitch propeller may lose rpm approaching a power-on stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].
Not foolproof, since you can stall in any attitude [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].
A stall may come with little or none of the usual cues [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].

body.p: An AOA indicator shows the otherwise 'invisible' AOA and its distance from the critical AOA, which the AFH calls stall margin awareness [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. In the PHAK sample calibration, the set points are zero on the ground, an optimum alpha at about 1.3 VS, and a cruise alpha at about VA [[1:125|PHAK 5-28]]. Limits: calibration technique, unheated probes or vanes, the type of indicator, flap setting (some indicators account for it, not all do) and wing contamination [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

callout.text: If your airplane has one, fly slow flight while watching it, so your target speed also becomes an AOA picture. The AFH encourages in-flight training with the indicator in slow flight, stalls, takeoffs and landings [[24:120|AFH 5-15]].

check.q: Name two things that can make an AOA indicator less reliable.
check.a: Any two of: calibration technique, unheated probes or vanes, the type of indicator, flap setting, wing contamination [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

chunks.title: Fly it: entry, configurations and maneuvering

body.p: A generic flow. Your POH/AFM gives the real limit speeds, stall speeds and any manufacturer altitude.

bullets: 1. Clear the area with clearing turns and say it: 'clear left, right, above and below' [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
2. Choose an entry altitude so the whole task, climbs and descents included, ends no lower than 1,500 ft AGL, or higher if the manufacturer recommends it [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
3. Reduce power from cruise and raise the nose to hold altitude as the speed decays. Listen for the change in airflow sound [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

4. Extend gear and flaps only at airspeeds within their limits; the before-landing checks set the landing configuration [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Anticipate the AOA change as the flaps move [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].
5. Approaching the target, add power to hold altitude, add right rudder, and trim off the back pressure [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
6. Hold the examiner's altitude, heading and airspeed with no stall warning: pitch for airspeed, power for the flightpath [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
7. Turns: coordinated aileron and rudder, and more power to hold altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
8. Climbs and climbing turns: add power and hold airspeed with pitch; climbing turns use a medium bank of about 20° [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
9. Descents and descending turns: reduce power and hold airspeed with pitch. AFH practice includes straight-ahead power-off gliding descents [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].
10. Exit only when told (next section).

head: What the examiner checks
Commercial ACS standard
rows: Task completed no lower than 1,500 ft AGL in a single-engine airplane (ACS CA.VII.A.S2)
A speed where more AOA, more load factor or less power would bring a stall warning; airspeed +5/-0 knots (ACS CA.VII.A.S3, S5)
Coordinated straight-and-level, turns, climbs and descents in the configuration the examiner names, without a stall warning (ACS CA.VII.A.S4)
Specified altitude ±50 ft, heading ±10°, bank ±5° (ACS CA.VII.A.S5)

callout.text: Flap and gear limit speeds, stall speeds for each configuration and any manufacturer's minimum altitude come from your POH/AFM. The AFH is general guidance only.

check.q: Why do you add power as you reach the target speed instead of keeping the reduced power you used to slow down?
check.a: Slow flight is well below L/DMAX, where flying slower takes more power; near the target speed additional power is needed to hold altitude [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

chunks.title: Exiting slow flight, and answering a stall warning

body.p: To exit, add power. As airspeed and lift build, apply forward pressure to lower the AOA and hold altitude, stay coordinated, level the wings and return to your flightpath. As the speed increases, retract flaps and gear, retrim, and anticipate the AOA change as they come up [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

callout.text: Abrupt or rough control movements in slow flight can stall the airplane; raising the flaps abruptly is the AFH's own example [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Nose-high trim and premature flap retraction are known causal factors in go-around stall/spin accidents [[13:11|AC 61-67C p5]].

body.p: If a stall warning does come on, you have left slow flight and reached the edge of a stall. The most important action is to reduce the AOA; pilots who put power and altitude first have lost control [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. In a training airplane with no autopilot or speedbrakes the AFH template shrinks to four steps: pitch nose-down until the warning stops, roll wings level, add power as needed, and return to the flightpath without a secondary stall [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

callout.text: Adding power reduces the altitude lost, but it does not stop a stall by itself. The AOA must come down [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

check.q: The horn sounds in a slow-flight climbing turn. Which comes first: leveling the wings or reducing the AOA?
check.a: Reducing the AOA. The AFH warns against controlling the bank before reducing AOA [[24:121|AFH 5-16]].

chunks.title: Turbulence, wind shear and density altitude

body.p: A vertical gust or wind shear suddenly changes the relative wind and can raise the AOA abruptly, so the airplane can stall at a much higher airspeed than in smooth air [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. In slow flight your margin is a few knots, and speed instability means a gust-caused speed loss keeps growing unless you act [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

Microbursts come from convective weather. They are often 1 to 2 miles across, last 5 to 15 minutes, and can produce downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm. A headwind turning into a tailwind cuts airspeed and performance [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]]. That is a poor match for an airplane already near the stall, so keep slow flight practice well away from storms and virga.

High density altitude reduces engine power, propeller thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. Indicated stall speed changes little with altitude, though true airspeed is higher [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. What you lose is excess power: the power available curve sits lower, so the point where power required beats power available comes sooner [[24:101|AFH 4-15]] [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

callout.text: Checkride note: turbulence may cause a momentary stall horn. Recognize it and correct promptly, and that alone is not unsatisfactory (ACS CA.VII.A, Appendix 3).
Application: in bumps, fly the top half of the +5/-0 window, make small corrections, and keep the ball centered.

check.q: At a hot, high practice area, does the indicated stall speed change much from sea level? What does change?
check.a: Not much; altitude has little or no effect on indicated stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. Power and thrust drop with density altitude, so there is less excess power [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]].

body.p: More than one-quarter (26.6 percent) of fatal accidents in the last 10 years happened in maneuvering flight, and maneuvering itself takes attention away from scanning [[16:12|AC 90-48E 11.2.2.1]]. In slow flight the nose is high, the airplane is slow, and you are busy.

bullets: Clear before you start and say the callouts: 'clear left, right, above and below' [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].
High wings hide traffic above and low wings hide traffic below; banking from time to time uncovers the blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

The AC suggests adjusting pitch in a climb to see over the nose, and gentle banks left and right in level flight or descents [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. Application: in slow flight a pitch change moves your airspeed, so use gentle coordinated banks to look around.
Scan in steps of no more than 10°, about 1 second each. Traffic with no relative motion is likely on a collision course [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].

body.p: Distractions: stalls from poor airspeed control are most likely when the pilot is busy with something else, such as finding a checklist, reading a chart, working fuel numbers or reaching for an item [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. Instructors use those same distractions in slow flight training: find a heading on a chart, reset the clock, read the outside air temperature, compute true airspeed, climb or descend 200 feet [[13:16|AC 61-67C p10]].

Orientation: keep outside references in view and cross-check the instruments [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Fixation on the instruments and poor division of attention between control and orientation are both on the AFH list of slow flight errors [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Prioritize: any task that pulls you away from AOA control can wait until you have exited slow flight.

callout.text: Outside, ball, airspeed, altitude. Then everything else.

check.q: You are in a high-wing airplane in slow flight. Where is your biggest blind spot, and how do you uncover it?
check.a: Above you. Banking from time to time uncovers blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

head: AFH error
How it shows on a checkride
Fix
rows: Clearing turns and callouts every time [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]]
Too little back pressure as power comes off
Altitude sinks past 50 ft during the slowdown
Raise the nose as the power comes back [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Too much back pressure as power comes off
A climb, then the speed falls fast toward the warning
Smaller pitch changes; on the backside a small pitch change is a big airspeed change [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]
Ball out, heading creeping left past 10°
More right rudder as power rises and speed falls [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Heading or bank wanders while airspeed is perfect
Altitude or speed jumps as the flaps move
Plan the pitch change; avoid abrupt flap retraction [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]
Chasing altitude with pitch, speed outside +5/-0
Power for altitude, pitch for airspeed [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]
Lost track of position or traffic
Short scans outside between instrument checks [[24:32|AFH 1-11]]
Strong back pressure and jerky pitch
Not responding to a stall warning
Holding the nose up through the horn

body.p: The error list is from [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]; the middle column applies the commercial tolerances (ACS CA.VII.A.S5).

callout.text: The slow side has no tolerance. If the speed decays even 1 knot below target, fix it right away with a little less pitch and a little more power, before the warning comes (ACS CA.VII.A.S5) [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

check.q: Your altitude is perfect but the airspeed is 2 knots below target. What has failed, and what fixes it?
check.a: Airspeed, which allows +5/-0 (ACS CA.VII.A.S5). Lower the nose slightly and add power to hold altitude; pitch is the airspeed control on the backside [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-3. Angle of attack at various speeds. (PHAK 5-3)
f1.alt: Three side views of the same airfoil in level flight, each with a flight path arrow pointing forward and a relative wind arrow pointing back. Level high speed: about 3 degrees angle of attack. Level cruise speed: about 6 degrees. Level low speed: about 12 degrees, with the airfoil tilted noticeably nose up.

f2.caption: Figure 11-14. Power required curve. (PHAK 11-12)
f2.alt: A graph of power setting against speed. A blue U-shaped power required curve sits under a red maximum power available curve, with the gap marked excess power. A vertical line at the lowest point of the U is marked best endurance speed, and the shaded area to its left, where the curve rises steeply toward low speed, is marked region of reversed command.

f3.caption: Figure 11-34. Stall speed table. (PHAK 11-28)
f3.alt: A stall speed table for a 2,750 lb airplane, by angle of bank. Gear and flaps up, power on, in knots: level 54, 30 degrees 58, 45 degrees 64, 60 degrees 76. Gear and flaps up, power off: 65, 70, 77, 92. Gear and flaps down, power on: 47, 50, 56, 66. Gear and flaps down, power off: 57, 62, 68, 81. MPH values are also shown.

f4.caption: Figure 4-14. The energy depletion scenario viewed in the power required and available curve. (AFH 4-15)
f4.alt: A power versus speed graph. A dashed power available curve for 8,000 feet and above arches low across the graph. A solid power required curve dips to a minimum and rises at both ends, very steeply at the slow end. Point A on the power available curve sits above the required curve; point B is where the curves cross on the slow side; point C, a little slower, is where power required is above power available. Speeds 1, 2 and 3 on the axis match these points, with 3 marked stall and 2 marked minimum level flight speed. A box marks the steep slow end as the region of irreversible rate of energy depletion.

f5.caption: Figure 5-51. Asymmetrical loading of propeller (P-factor). (PHAK 5-33)
f5.alt: Two side views of a high-wing airplane's nose and propeller. At low angle of attack the airflow arrows meet the propeller straight on and the load arrows on the upward and downward moving blades are equal. At high angle of attack, nose up, the arrow for the downward moving blade is larger than the arrow for the upward moving blade.

f6.caption: Figure 5-9. A conceptual representation of an AOA indicator. (AFH 5-14)
f6.alt: Three panels of an airfoil in airflow. A at 10 degrees has smooth flow. B at 16 degrees shows flow starting to break away behind the wing. C at 17 degrees shows heavy turbulent separation over the top. Three matching AOA indicator displays: A shows a blue circle, B shows red chevrons above it, C shows a single red chevron at the top. A lift coefficient graph shows A partway up a straight line and B and C at the top, where the line peaks near 2.0 and turns down.

scenario.title: The slow orbit over the job site
scenario.setup: You are a new commercial pilot hired to fly a photographer over a construction site. The airplane is a four-seat high-wing single with a fixed-pitch propeller and a stall horn. You are near maximum weight, and with the photographer and a heavy camera bag in back the CG is near the aft limit. The area elevation is 4,800 ft and the temperature is 32°C. The client wants slow, steady orbits so the photographer can shoot. Afternoon cumulus is building to the south, and another airplane is doing photo work in the same area.

questions.q: Why is this job a setup for inadvertent slow flight?
questions.a: A slow, steady orbit puts you at low speed and high AOA while your attention is split between the site, the photographer and traffic. Stalls from poor airspeed control happen most when the pilot is busy with other tasks [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]], and maneuvering flight accounts for more than a quarter of fatal accidents [[16:12|AC 90-48E 11.2.2.1]].

questions.q: How do the weight, the aft CG and the orbit's bank change your stall margin?
questions.a: More weight raises the stall speed [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. An aft CG takes less elevator force to reach the stall, so an accidental stall comes easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]]. The bank adds load factor, and stall speed rises with its square root [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]].

questions.q: What does the hot, high area do to the slow end of your envelope?
questions.a: High density altitude reduces power, thrust and lift [[1:91|PHAK 4-4]]. With less power available, power required can exceed power available at the slow end, and the way out is to give up altitude for speed [[24:102|AFH 4-16]].

questions.q: The photographer asks you to slow down 'just a bit more' in the turn, and you hold altitude with back pressure. What is happening aerodynamically?
questions.a: You are adding AOA in a bank that already adds load factor, and in slow flight any further increase in either brings the stall warning [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Below L/DMAX the speed keeps decaying unless you reduce AOA or add power [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

questions.q: You notice you have been holding left rudder to tighten the orbit toward the site, and the ball is out. Why does that matter?
questions.a: That is a skid. Exceeding the critical AOA with excessive rudder is the primary cause of inadvertent spins, and a spin from a skid rotates in the direction of the controls [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]]. The airspeed indicator and altimeter are also unreliable when uncoordinated [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

questions.q: How do you handle the other photo airplane and the building cumulus?
questions.a: Scan in short steps and bank from time to time to see past the high wing [[24:32|AFH 1-11]] [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. Stay well clear of the cumulus: microbursts can bring downdrafts up to 6,000 fpm and sudden airspeed losses [[1:295|PHAK 12-11]].

skills.do: Clear the area before slowing down, with clearing turns and a visible scan.
skills.practice: Make your clearing turns and say 'clear left, right, above and below' every time [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] [[1:362|PHAK 14-28]].

skills.do: Choose an entry altitude so the whole task, including descents, ends at or above 1,500 ft AGL.
skills.practice: Before each flight, find the highest terrain in the practice area and add 1,500 ft plus your planned descents [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

skills.do: Hold an airspeed just above the stall warning, where more AOA, more load factor or less power would set it off, at the speed the examiner specifies.
skills.practice: In each configuration, slow to the warning, lower the nose slightly until it stops, add power to hold altitude, and note that airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

skills.do: Fly coordinated straight-and-level flight, turns, climbs and descents in the configuration the examiner names, with no stall warning.
skills.practice: Practice each one in landing, takeoff and clean configurations, keeping the ball centered as the power changes [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

skills.do: Hold altitude within 50 ft, heading within 10°, airspeed from the target to 5 knots above it, and bank within 5° of the specified bank.
skills.practice: Have your CFI call out every deviation of more than half the tolerance, and sometimes fly with the airspeed indicator covered as AC 61-67C suggests [[13:16|AC 61-67C p10]].

quiz.q: How does the commercial ACS airspeed tolerance for slow flight compare with the private?
options: +5/-0 knots commercial, +10/-0 knots private
Plus or minus 5 knots for both
+10/-0 knots commercial, +10/-5 knots private
Plus or minus 10 knots commercial, +5/-0 knots private
quiz.why: Commercial is +5/-0 knots (ACS CA.VII.A.S5); private is +10/-0 knots (ACS PA.VII.A.S5).

quiz.q: Which slow-flight tolerance is the same for private and commercial applicants?
options: Heading, plus or minus 10°
Altitude
Bank angle
Airspeed
quiz.why: Heading is plus or minus 10° in both. Altitude goes from 100 to 50 ft, bank from 10° to 5°, and airspeed from +10/-0 to +5/-0 (ACS CA.VII.A.S5) (ACS PA.VII.A.S5).

quiz.q: In the PHAK example of one wing in level flight, what is the AOA at low speed compared with cruise?
options: About 12° at low speed, about 6° at cruise
About 6° at low speed, about 12° at cruise
About 3° at low speed, about 6° at cruise
The same AOA; only the airspeed changes
quiz.why: Figure 5-3 shows about 3° at high speed, 6° at cruise and 12° at low speed [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]].

quiz.q: A published 1G stall speed is valid only under certain conditions. Which of these is NOT one of them?
options: Any bank angle up to 30°
Unaccelerated 1G flight
Coordinated flight, ball centered
One weight, typically maximum gross
quiz.why: The AFH lists unaccelerated 1G flight, coordinated flight, one weight and one CG [[24:118|AFH 5-13]]. Any bank in a level turn adds load factor, and stall speed rises with its square root [[1:131|PHAK 5-34]].

quiz.q: What is one AFH way to find your slow-flight target airspeed in a given configuration?
options: Slow to the stall warning, lower the nose slightly until it stops, add power to hold altitude, and note the airspeed
Add 30 knots to the published clean stall speed
Use VY in every configuration
Slow until the full stall, then add 2 knots
quiz.why: That is the method the AFH gives for finding the target airspeed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]]. Its general guide is 5 to 10 knots above the 1G stall speed [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

quiz.q: Where does the PHAK place the start of the region of reversed command?
options: Below the speed for minimum power required (best endurance speed)
Below VA
Below VY
Only below the stall warning speed
quiz.why: Speeds below the speed for maximum endurance, the lowest point on the power curve, need higher power as speed drops [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]].

quiz.q: According to the AFH energy model, the throttle mainly controls:
options: The airplane's total energy
Airspeed only
Altitude only
How energy is split between altitude and airspeed
quiz.why: The throttle is the total energy controller; the elevator distributes energy between altitude and airspeed [[24:90|AFH 4-4]].

quiz.q: The corkscrew slipstream pushes hardest on the vertical fin when:
options: Power is high and forward speed is low
Power is low and speed is high
In a power-off glide
At cruise speed
quiz.why: At high propeller speed and low forward speed the spiral is compact and exerts a strong sideward force on the fin [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

quiz.q: In the PHAK sample AOA indicator calibration, the optimum alpha set point matches about what airspeed?
options: 1.3 VS
VA
VS exactly
VNE
quiz.why: The sample set points are zero on the ground, optimum alpha at about 1.3 x VS, and cruise alpha at about VA [[1:125|PHAK 5-28]].

quiz.q: Your airplane is in slow flight and a bump knocks the airspeed down 2 knots. Because of speed instability, what happens next?
options: The speed keeps falling unless you lower the AOA or add power
The speed returns to trim by itself
The airplane speeds up because drag drops
The airplane climbs
quiz.why: Below L/DMAX, a speed loss can keep growing without pilot action [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]; the speed loss raises drag, which lowers speed further [[24:386|AFH G-14]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner asks for straight-and-level slow flight at 4,000 ft, heading 240°, 58 knots. Which set of readings passes the commercial standard?
final_quiz.why: 45 ft low, 8° off and 4 knots fast are all inside ±50 ft, ±10° and +5/-0. The others fail altitude (60 ft high), airspeed (1 knot slow) or heading (12° off) (ACS CA.VII.A.S5). AFH lists inadequate power management and altitude loss from back-elevator errors as slow flight errors [[24:117|AFH 5-12]].

final_quiz.q: The examiner specifies a 20° bank for a slow-flight turn. What is the steepest bank you may show and still pass?
options: 20° exactly
final_quiz.why: Bank tolerance is plus or minus 5° at the commercial level, so 15° to 25° (ACS CA.VII.A.S5). AFH says to practice turns in slow flight and add power during them to hold altitude [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].

final_quiz.q: Using the PHAK sample table, you are in clean slow flight with power on at 62 knots. The examiner asks for a level 45° bank turn. What does the table predict?
options: The stall speed rises to 64 knots, above your airspeed, so a stall warning or stall is likely
Nothing changes power-on
The stall speed falls to 58 knots
Only the landing configuration stall speed changes with bank
final_quiz.why: Clean, power on: 54 knots level, 64 knots at 45° [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. That is above your 62 knots. Slow-flight turns use medium banks, about 20° for climbing turns [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

final_quiz.q: Hot and high, you are at full power in slow flight, yet the airspeed is creeping down and you are slowly losing altitude. What does the AFH say gets you out?
options: Lower the nose to trade some altitude for speed, then climb once there is excess power
Raise the nose to stop the descent
Add more flaps for more lift
Hold the attitude and wait for the engine to catch up
final_quiz.why: With power available below power required, first trade altitude for speed to reach positive excess power, then climb [[24:102|AFH 4-16]] [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

final_quiz.q: On a short-field power approach you develop an unacceptably high sink rate. In the region of reversed command, what does the PHAK say can reduce or stop it?
options: Applying power
Lowering the nose with no power
Raising the nose with no power
Reducing power and flaring early
final_quiz.why: Power may stop the descent; lowering the nose without power gives a rapid sink and altitude loss [[1:268|PHAK 11-12]].

final_quiz.q: In slow flight you are 30 ft low with the airspeed exactly on target. What does the AFH say it takes to climb back without changing the airspeed?
options: Throttle forward while easing back on the yoke, together
Elevator alone
Throttle alone
Lower the nose first, then add power
final_quiz.why: Changing altitude without changing speed needs both controls at once [[24:99|AFH 4-13]].

final_quiz.q: You roll into a slow-flight right turn using aileron only. Which way does the nose first yaw, and why?
options: Left, because the rising left wing has more drag
Right, because the lowered wing pulls it
Left, because of gyroscopic precession
Neither way; adverse yaw only happens at high speed
final_quiz.why: The rising wing gets more lift and more drag, yawing the nose opposite to the turn; rudder with aileron cancels it [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your airplane has no stall horn, only natural buffet, and you practice slow-flight descents at idle. Why be extra careful?
options: Power-off stall cues are less noticeable than power-on cues
Buffet is stronger power-off, so it may startle you
The critical AOA is lower with power off
Descents cannot lead to a stall
final_quiz.why: Power-off buffeting and shaking are less noticeable than power-on [[24:120|AFH 5-15]], and the warning in such airplanes comes only from the airframe's own buffet [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

final_quiz.q: Your rental airplane has an AOA indicator. Before trusting it in slow flight with full flaps, what should you find out?
options: Whether that indicator takes flap position into account
Whether it was calibrated at VNE
Whether it reads in knots
Nothing; AOA indicators are not affected by flaps
final_quiz.why: Some indicators take flap position into consideration, but not all do; flap setting is a listed limitation [[24:118|AFH 5-13]] [[24:119|AFH 5-14]].

final_quiz.q: A friend says, 'Pull the power back, hold the nose up until the horn chirps, and fly right there.' What is wrong with that for your commercial checkride?
options: The ACS requires maneuvering without a stall warning with airspeed +5/-0
Nothing; flying on the horn is the standard
The horn must be switched off for the test
Slow flight must be flown clean only
final_quiz.why: S4 requires maneuvering without a stall warning and S5 allows airspeed +5/-0 knots (ACS CA.VII.A.S4, S5). A required stall warning device should not be deactivated for a practical test [[13:22|AC 61-67C p16]].

final_quiz.q: While you change a radio frequency in slow flight, the bank grows to 28° in a turn meant for 20°, and the airspeed drops 2 knots below target. What do you do?
options: Fly first: shallow the bank, lower the AOA slightly and add power, then finish the frequency
Finish the frequency, then fix it
Add full power only
Pull back to stop any altitude loss
final_quiz.why: Stalls from poor airspeed control happen when pilots are busy with other tasks [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. Bank and speed are both out of tolerance (ACS CA.VII.A.S5), and more bank means more load factor [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]].

final_quiz.q: Why does a nose-high, high-power slow-flight attitude change how much the wing has to lift?
options: Part of the thrust acts upward and supports some of the weight
The propeller adds weight to the nose
The horizontal tail lifts the airplane
It does not; thrust never helps support the airplane
final_quiz.why: In the nose-high attitude a vertical component of thrust helps support the airplane, so wing loading is less than expected [[1:100|PHAK 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: A passenger loads a heavy suitcase in the aft baggage area, moving the CG aft but within limits. What changes in slow flight?
options: Less elevator force reaches the stall, so an accidental stall is easier
The stall speed drops, so slow flight is safer
Only cruise speed changes
The stall horn sounds sooner
final_quiz.why: As the CG moves aft, less elevator deflection is needed to stall, so inadvertent stall entry is easier [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]]. Small balance changes can also affect spin characteristics [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

takeaways: Slow flight sits just above the stall warning: more AOA, more G or less power sets it off.
Commercial window: altitude ±50 ft, heading ±10°, airspeed +5/-0 knots, bank ±5°, and no stall warning.
The critical AOA never moves. The stall speed moves with load factor, weight, CG, flaps and power.
In the region of reversed command, slower takes more power, and a speed loss feeds on itself.
Throttle sets total energy and the elevator splits it. When very slow, lower the AOA before expecting power to help.
High power and high AOA bring left yaw. Keep the ball centered with right rudder.
Any stall warning: reduce the AOA first, then level the wings and add power.
cfi_notes: The AFH and PHAK put the point where slower starts to take more power at different speeds. The AFH says it is below L/DMAX, the minimum drag speed [[24:115|AFH 5-10]]. The PHAK says it is below the best endurance speed, the lowest point of the power required curve, and calls that the region of reversed command [[1:267|PHAK 11-11]]. Slow flight is well below both speeds, so the difference does not change how you fly it.

AC 61-67C's stall-avoidance drill has the student hold heading and altitude with the stall warning device activated [[13:15|AC 61-67C p9]]. That AC predates the current ACS, which wants slow flight without a stall warning (ACS CA.VII.A.S3, S4). Keep the AC's distraction and covered-airspeed drills, not the on-the-horn part.

S3 describes a speed just above the warning, while S5 holds the applicant to airspeed +5/-0 (ACS CA.VII.A.S3, S5). Have students find the warning speed in each configuration with the AFH method [[24:114|AFH 5-9]] so they know how much room the examiner's number leaves.

Teach a spoken response for the Appendix 3 case: 'Horn, lowering AOA.' Recognition plus a prompt correction is what turns a momentary horn in turbulence into an acceptable event (ACS CA.VII.A, Appendix 3).

The PHAK stall speed table [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]] is the best tool for explaining why a power reduction is a stall-warning trigger: power-on and power-off stall speeds differ by about 10 knots in the landing configuration. It is a sample airplane; repeat the exercise with your own POH.

The AFH energy depletion scenario (Figure 4-14) is told with a twin [[24:101|AFH 4-15]], but the power-curve lesson applies to any airplane. Use it for high density altitude discussions and to show why lowering the nose is the way out.

The AFH points to AC 120-109 for stall prevention and recovery training [[24:132|AFH 5-27]], but that AC is not among this lesson's sources. The stall content here comes from the AFH, PHAK and AC 61-67C.

If the airplane has an AOA indicator, use it in slow flight. AC 61-98E asks flight instructors to evaluate its use in flight reviews and to stress AOA knowledge when none is installed [[15:27|AC 61-98E 4.3.4]].
gaps: Airplane-specific numbers come from the POH/AFM: stall speeds for each configuration, where the stall warning starts, flap and gear limit speeds, and any manufacturer's minimum altitude. The PHAK table is only a sample [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]].
Current Part 23 requires a stall warning with 'sufficient margin' but gives no number [[60:103|14 CFR 23.2150]]; the 4 to 8 knot figure comes from an older AC [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].
No source quantifies how much the slow-flight margin shrinks in turbulence or at high density altitude for a light single. The sources describe the effects only in general terms.
The sources give no pitch attitudes, power settings or rudder amounts for slow flight. Those come from the POH and CFI demonstration.
AOA indicator calibration and flap handling depend on the installation; the PHAK set points are a sample [[1:125|PHAK 5-28]]. Check the manufacturer's information.

The ACS objective says 'cruise configuration,' but S4 says the configuration is specified by the evaluator (ACS CA.VII.A.S4), and the AFH says slow flight is typically evaluated in the landing configuration [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Be ready for any configuration.

activities.title: Work the stall speed numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Sample table (Figure 11-34): gear and flaps down, power on, wings level. You plan slow flight 7 knots above the stall speed. What is your target airspeed?
items.why: The table gives 47 knots. 47 + 7 = 54 knots [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. That fits the AFH's 5 to 10 knot guide [[24:114|AFH 5-9]].

items.q: At that 54 knots you pull the power to idle and hold altitude. The power-off stall speed in the same configuration is 57 knots. How many knots below the power-off stall speed are you?
items.why: 57 - 54 = 3 knots below it [[1:284|PHAK 11-28]]. That is why a reduction in power is one of the stall-warning triggers (ACS CA.VII.A.S3).

items.q: Check the table with the load factor rule. Clean, power off, wings level: 65 knots. Load factor in a level 30° bank is 1 / cos 30°, and stall speed rises with its square root. What is the stall speed at 30°?
Landing configuration, power on, wings level: 47 knots. About what is the stall speed in a 20° climbing turn? (Load factor = 1 / cos 20°.)
items.why: 1 / cos 20° = 1 / 0.940 = 1.064 G. Square root = 1.032. 47 x 1.032 = 48.5 knots [[13:8|AC 61-67C p2]]. The 20° bank the AFH uses for climbing turns [[24:115|AFH 5-10]] costs only about 1.5 knots of margin.

items.q: Lift is proportional to the square of velocity. By what factor must the lift coefficient rise to keep the same lift when you slow from 100 knots to 50 knots?
items.why: (100 / 50) squared = 2 squared = 4 [[1:101|PHAK 5-4]]. The pilot gets the higher lift coefficient by raising the AOA, up to the critical AOA.

activities.title: Read the energy depletion curve
activities.intro: Drag each label to its numbered pin.

pins.label: Climbing: power available is more than power required
Stall horn: power required is more than power available
Least power needed for level flight
Slow end: each knot slower takes much more power
Front side: more speed takes more power

activities.title: Throttle or elevator?
activities.intro: Tap an error, then tap the control the AFH uses to fix it.
buckets: Total energy error: fix mainly with the throttle
Distribution error: fix mainly with the elevator

items.t: Lower and slower on final approach
Higher and slower after a gust
Climbing and speeding up after too much power
Descending and speeding up after the nose dropped

activities.title: Name the yawing and rolling effect
activities.intro: Tap an effect, then what causes it.

pairs.r: The airplane tries to roll opposite to the propeller's rotation
A compact spiral of air pushes on the vertical fin at high power and low speed
A force on the propeller disc acts 90° ahead in the direction of rotation
The downgoing blade makes more thrust than the upgoing blade at high AOA
The rising wing's extra drag yaws the nose away from the turn

activities.title: True or false: stall warning and AOA
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: Part 23 requires a clear and distinctive stall warning with enough margin to prevent an inadvertent stall.
VSW is the speed at which a natural or artificial stall warning begins.
cards.why: True. That is the 14 CFR definition [[60:21|14 CFR 1.2]].

cards.s: Pitch attitude alone is a foolproof cue that a stall is coming.
cards.why: False. The airplane can be stalled in any attitude, so vision is not a foolproof cue, though pitch awareness still matters [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: Every AOA indicator automatically corrects for flap position.
cards.why: False. Some indicators take flap position into account, but not all do [[24:118|AFH 5-13]].

cards.s: Approaching a power-on stall, a fixed-pitch propeller may lose rpm.
cards.why: True. Loss of rpm may be evident in fixed-pitch airplanes approaching a power-on stall [[13:10|AC 61-67C p4]].

cards.s: On the commercial checkride, any momentary stall horn caused by turbulence is automatically unsatisfactory.
cards.why: False. If you recognize it and correct promptly, a momentary activation is not unsatisfactory (ACS CA.VII.A, Appendix 3).

activities.title: The stall recovery template, in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the AFH template steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Disconnect the autopilot or wing leveler, if equipped
Pitch nose-down until the stall warning stops
Trim nose-down if the elevator alone does not do it
Retract speedbrakes or spoilers, if equipped
Return to the desired flightpath without a secondary stall

activities.title: Slow flight on the checkride, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are on your commercial checkride in a single-engine high-wing airplane with a fixed-pitch propeller. Terrain in the practice area is about 1,800 ft MSL. The examiner says: 'Slow flight, landing configuration, 3,800 feet, heading 180, 55 knots. Then a climbing turn to the left, and a descent.'

steps.s: Before you start, what do you check about 3,800 ft?
options: That it leaves room for the climb and descent to finish at or above 1,500 ft AGL
Nothing; the examiner picked it
That it is at least 3,000 ft AGL, as for any slow flight
Only that it is below the clouds
steps.why: S2 requires an entry altitude that lets the task finish no lower than 1,500 ft AGL in a single-engine airplane (ACS CA.VII.A.S2). 3,800 - 1,800 = 2,000 ft AGL, so the floor is 3,300 ft MSL. The 3,000 ft figure is for multiengine airplanes [[24:115|AFH 5-10]].

steps.s: Slowing through 70 knots as the flaps come down, the altimeter reads 3,860 ft and the airspeed is falling fast.
options: Add power to stop the climb
Relax some back pressure to stop the climb and settle back to 3,800, then add power near 55 knots
Pull more to slow down faster
Raise the flaps to stop the balloon
steps.why: Too much back pressure as power comes off gives a climb, then a rapid speed loss [[24:117|AFH 5-12]]. Higher and slower is a distribution error fixed with the elevator [[24:98|AFH 4-12]]. Near the target you will need more power [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. 60 ft high is already outside the 50 ft window (ACS CA.VII.A.S5).

steps.s: Stable at 3,800 ft and 56 knots, you add full power and start the left climbing turn. The nose yaws left and the ball slides right.
options: More right rudder
More left rudder to tighten the turn
Reduce the power
More left aileron
steps.why: High power at low speed brings a strong left yaw from torque, slipstream and P-factor, which needs right rudder [[24:116|AFH 5-11]]. Exceeding the critical AOA while uncoordinated is the primary cause of inadvertent spins [[13:12|AC 61-67C p6]].

steps.s: In the turn a gust bumps the airplane and the stall horn chirps once.
options: Ignore it; it was only a chirp
Release a little back pressure to lower the AOA, then regain the target speed and bank
Add full power and pull to hold altitude
Roll the wings level first, then check the airspeed
steps.why: Any stall warning: reduce AOA first [[24:120|AFH 5-15]]. A gust can raise the AOA abruptly [[13:9|AC 61-67C p3]]. A momentary horn in turbulence is acceptable only when you recognize it and correct promptly (ACS CA.VII.A, Appendix 3).

steps.s: Level again after the descent, the examiner says, 'Return to cruise.'
options: Raise all the flaps, then add power
Add power, use forward pressure as the speed builds, then raise the flaps in steps and retrim
Lower the nose steeply to gain speed, then add power
Add power and hold the nose high until cruise speed
steps.why: Exit by adding power, then forward pressure to hold altitude as speed and lift build; clean up as the airspeed increases and anticipate the AOA change. Raising the flaps abruptly can stall the airplane [[24:116|AFH 5-11]].
